Games becoming easier over the years is an interesting discussion. Were games too hard? Were they legitimatly hard on the nes? Snes? But difficult games are not gone completely. Games like dark souls and blood bourne show people still enjoy testing their limits. If those games names make you shutter at the thought of playing them due to the difficulty then this isn't a game for you. But to me? I love this game. It's a challanging platformer and yet...I almost never felt frustrated. But to start off, here we go.

Graphics 10/10-They're very pleasing to look at. Very minimalistic and not taxing on your hardware. I enjoy the little touches like blood trails on where you walk or climb. Don't expect ground breaking, but I don't think that was the intent.

Sound 10/10- Sound tracks are good. And never really repetitive. And the death sounds are gross in the best way possible.

controls 10/10-Perfect. Period. And it needs to be. If the controls were even a little bit off, it would be unplayable due to the pin point accuracy you need to get through the game. Ironicly the controls are so perfect you will need to get used to them. There is NO delay and that may throw you off for a little bit. But I never felt like the controls messed me up.

Gameplay 9/10-I love it. But it's really hard. I cannot say this enough. You need so much practice and such great reflexes, that you may not be able to beat the game. My point is that this game isn't for everyone. But this game does make it less frustrating by respawning you when you die at once. And the levels are not long either meaning you can get back to where you died quickly. Unlimited lives as well. My only problem is the hidden levels that have lives. It seems counter intuitive to the idea of the game and doesn't seem like a good idea.But it's so rewarding when you beat a level, it just feels unmatched. 

replay 10/10- Yes, this will last you a while. unlockable characters with their own abilities,hidden levels and a harder dark world to complete...you get the bang for your buck.

overall 10/10-This isn't for everyone. But with it's perfect controls, great level design, and dark sense of humor, I always had fun even when I died, a lot.

Ok, Let me start off saying i absolutely adore Super Meat Boy. It's got great level design, funny humour and plenty of well-made content to enjoy.

HOWEVER

I simply cannot recommend the steam version due to the consistent issue of the game deleting Save data for literally no reason. When this happened to me i kept looking to see if others had the same issue and as it turns out, i'm not alone and in fact i found a thread from 2012 talking about experiencing this bug. 2012. And it still is in the game and is a common issue. To make it clear how long that was ago, This game is a decade old, so a game-breaking bug was left in for a decade despite numerous patches. To say this is inexcusable is an under-statement and because of this i beg of you to get it physically for PC or on console. This is Friggin Stupid.

For those of you who haven't played this yet, be warned. They're not kidding when they said this game was very hard! But aside from the high difficulty of this game, everything else is awesome. The soundtrack, the retro video games, the playable characters from other games, and I especially love the idea of the Dark World which clones all the main levels but made harder! If you are planning to buy this game, I suggest picking up the soundtrack too. What's an indie game without a zany soundtrack?

But let me tell you this one other thing: Practice makes perfect. With hours of practice and thousands of meat boys dying, you could negotiate the far reaches of the game and maybe even get the ironman achievements! I recommend this game because of the above-ness.

Super Meat Boy is a the creme de la creme of 2D challenging platformers. It stands out head and shoulders above the rest. It has a beautiful art style, cut scenes parodying old Nintendo games and a simple plot. A villain has taken Bandage Girl and you as Super Meat Boy must reach her at the end of every single level. When you get to her she gets whisked away time and time again. The 7 'chapters' each have around 20 levels that can get completed in 30 seconds or less. The real challenge here is that most everything causes instant death. Spikes, grinders, guns and pits. With each death, you respawn at the start with no load time. This keeps you in the game. Every chapter has its own theme including a forest, a hospital, a salt factory and even Hell itself. At the end of every level is a new and unique boss fight that usually consists of a race.

Even if people have branded it a difficult game, you will eventually get through the game with enough practice. Since there are no lives and you just respawn, there is no consequence. While completing a level just leads to the next level, there is an easy to use map so you can go back and replay areas. On top of that, for every 'grade A' (under par time) that you get for a level, you can play its dark world counterpart making levels tougher. In all around 300 levels.

Each level has their own gimmicks. Platform riding, touch bricks that dissolve, raising lava, shooting saw blades, conveyer belts and so on. Some levels even have keys that when touched they remove lock blocks automatically. There is a lot of variety here. The game ratchets up up the creativity with portals. Since Meat Boy is one block tall, he can fit most anywhere. Some levels have winding paths through factories. Others are broad jumps between conveyer belts that launch him into the area. There are warp zones to find in levels that will send you to far more difficult levels. All with simple controls.

As a square of meat, the controls are simple, left, right, jump and run. You can even jump off walls and slide down them. Sometimes your wall jump will slide you up from momentum. Other than that the game isn't slippery like other 2D platformers. Meat Boy can stop on a dime. Holding run and jump can fly you across the screen to where you need to be. The Steam version has plenty of unlockable characters from collecting band-aids in certain levels. You'll also get to play as other characters that have different abilities. At the end of each level you're treated to seeing all your failed attempts playing all at once.

There's not much to say about the game. Its charm, art and music make it more desirable to play than the average 2D challenging platformer. Super Meat Boy has a lot of content for your money, complete with a level designer to unlock. So many people like something that makes them throw their controllers.

A lot of people love this game, so there's no real need to add another review to the thousands of others. However if this does get read by someone, it's worth it to add - less of a typical review but more so two personal ideas. 

Note I 106% completed this game on ps4 as I prefer the dual shock 4. I have limited hours on the steam version, but it's safe to say it's exactly the same experience (except for the music - steam has slightly better soundtrack, as well as different character unlockables).

-    First point (I think the most important) - this game essentially drew my attention back to the gaming industry. 

-    Second point - This game is a gateway (it was for me) to other challenging games.

First point - my attention was raised, I researched games again, I read books about the industry's history, and proudly began to play games with more effort and generally just play more games in general (mostly platformers admittedly). I firmly attribute my love of Super meat boy towards my refound love of all gaming.

Prior to even attempting super meat boy, I didn't play platformers often - I had super mario land as a young kid and along with the crash bandicoot series I only really played these two franchises of platformers. I didn't complete them as a kid, I just enjoyed them enough. As I grew up, I would play gta, saints row, gran turismo, tekken... And then all but gave up gaming from mid high school through the end of university. Very casual, mainstream games. Very limited hours invested...  

Then three years ago (approx) I found super meat boy... 

Catch up to today and I've bought old nintendo consoles, old playstations (the ones I didn't have or had sold) and went bananas and bought platformers galore. What's more is I play them, and appreciate them. The jumping arc, the speed, momentum, the wall jump, weight, gravity, just the sheer joy in movement, the flow. I love it all, but it was only after meat boy that I paid attention to these dynamics in all games in general. I analyse the moveset in 2d games, 3d games, platformers, racers (sim and arcade), skating games, twin stick shooters, shooters, old arcade games. Anything that focuses on movement.

I attribute it all, my love for gaming as an adult, but especially how they flow and feel, to Super meat boy. 

Second point - this game made me, forced me, to play other games of revered difficulty. I used to suck as gaming. This was due to lack of interest and practice, not innate skill. Super meat boy WILL improve your play, it will make you more determined, and will force you to persevere. You, as I did, will return to earlier levels in the game and clear worlds with no deaths. I humbly learned what my limits were, pushed them, and they grew. Yours will too. It will be work, but you'll love it. If you hate it, all the time, don't play platformers! Or maybe it just doesn't click. That's fine. But while you're raging away just recall how you can now fly through a previous devil of a 20 level world, and enjoyed doing so.. Leave the game. Tomorrow it will be there to fight. 

So that essentially sums up my attitude towards this and other difficult games, after playing super meat boy. I used to stop after a while and give up hard games. I've now near 100% completed many games because I want to. I'm not a super gamer, I just love them.
 
Thanks for reading. Enjoy the game.

Super Meat Boy doesn't try to be a lot, and as a result it is extremely good at what it does. Compared to other platforming games, there are no secrets, NPCs, or plotlines beyond Dr. Fetus doing something silly. But when it comes to gameplay, I haven't seen any game as good.

This game has extremely simple controls which makes getting better extremely satisfying. Throughout the game you unlock new characters but each comes with it's own upsides and downsides. There is no undisputed best character. All progression in the game comes from you building up your own skill, with basically no skill ceiling.

I genuinely believe this is the greatest platforming video game of all time. Just by playing casually, by the time you get 106% you will feel accomplished having completing a very difficult but not unreasonable task. That isn't where your skill progression ends though, as this game is ripe for speedrunning. Optimizing your movement to waste as little time as possible is extremely satisfying. Finding micro-optimizations like stopping before turning around or jumping through tight gaps to skip a few seconds from the intended route and putting them together into a single fast run is what makes this game so replayable.

Even if you never go down the speedrunning route, or even if you just get the light ending and ignore the dark worlds, you will still have had fun. But for the people out there who like challenges, this game offers so much room to grow in a way I haven't seen another game be able to replicate.

So, this is certainly a hard game. It more than lives up to its reputation as a pioneering precision platformer. The controls take a while to get used to, but this is nothing insurmountable. You will likely get frustrated while playing through the game, but that's what you signed up for, and the game isn't so bad that you don't want to keep playing another day when you finish your session. Overall, it's a pretty good game.

Until you start going for 100% completion. Then you have to deal with warp zones. And that's where everything goes downhill.

Hidden in some of the regular levels are portals to warp zones. You usually have to get to them rather quickly, as they will disappear after a period of time. This is not my problem with warp zones. It is just another challenge to finish.

Upon making it to one of these portals, you will be transported into a warp zone. 25% of the time, this warp zone will force you to play through a few levels as a new character. Upon completion of the warp zone, you unlock this character for use in regular gameplay. This is not my problem with warp zones. It is a cool gimmick that makes unlocking characters a little more interesting than collecting a bunch of bandages.

The remaining 75% of the time, you will be sent to a regular warp zone. These zones make you play through a series of three levels as Meat Boy. For each level, you have three lives. If you lose all your lives, you are kicked out of the warp zone and sent back to the map. This is not my problem with warp zones. Warp zones that you have visited are playable directly from the map.

When you start a level in a warp zone, a screen displays for a couple of seconds showing you which level you're on and how many lives you have remaining. This is my problem with warp zones. This right here. The extra two seconds of delay between deaths quickly gets very annoying. When you die, especially in a precision platformer, you should be able to jump (no pun intended) right back into the action. You should not have to wait two seconds to try again. Game overs are even worse. The game over screen is skippable, but should you wish to try again, you must watch Meat Boy get sucked into the warp zone for a couple of seconds and then look at the lives screen again. The lives screen is not skippable. It should be. It only takes a decisecond or two to take in the information the lives screen provides. In fact, you probably know it already. The lives screen completely ruins any fun you could possibly have with warp zones.

What's more, if you want to get all 100 bandages, you have to play these warp zones, as each regular warp zone contains two bandages. The character warp zones don't have this problem (as far as I remember), since they do not have a lives screen or life counter; only an amusing animation introducing the character you will be playing as. The rest of them, though, are a disgrace to an otherwise great game. Since warp zones are such a small feature in the grand scheme of things, I'd still recommend it, but be warned: the warp zones will make you more frustrated than anything else in any precision platformer.

At the release of Super Meat Boy back when, this game quickly cemented itself as one of *the* platformers that any gamer worth their salt had to play. Only having a keyboard I floundered around in the more difficult levels but still managed to get to the 5th world, where I dropped the game for a while due to its difficulty & precision.

I finally made that final push today with my controller, and where these levels that were quite brutal on younger me, it really dawned on present me on what makes this game so fun. This is already a classic - secret unlockable characters from other franchises, a soundtrack that holds up really well years later, and an honestly great approach to platforming I really wish I saw in more games.

This approach being, any death you're thrown right back into the level instantly. But the game saves every attempt and once you beat the level, you can watch every failed attempt at the same time from the pov of your successful attempt, watching you fail the same jump 20 times just to see that one lucky run thread that needle where the rest have failed. So even if a level is super frustrating, not giving up just to see that one successful attempt makes such a brutal and challenging game so rewarding.

This game definitely didn't hold any punches back, simply completing the game has such a low completion rate let alone any achievements that demand a mastery of its content. This game is not for everyone - but anyone who wants a challenge should definitely try to see the main game to the end.

Probably the greatest 2D platformer ever made.

Run and jump. That's what you get. No attacks, no special abilities (outside of unlockable characters), and no powerups. Platforming distilled to its purest elements, and executed flawlessly. 

No other game is this fun to control. That includes Celeste and any Mario game. 

There are no stats or upgrades. You progress by getting better. There is no other option. 

Danny Baronowski's soundtrack is stellar and catchy while also reflecting the feelings of the worlds. For this reason, the newer console versions are far inferior since they contain a different, and much worse, soundtrack. 

A note on the difficulty: A very difficult game, but probably the most fair of any "extreme difficulty" game I've played. There are no poorly telegraphed traps, hidden hazards, or trick platforms. You can see anything that can kill you far before it actually kills you. Additionally, once you die, you respawn in under a second, so you're already on your next attempt before you have the time to be mad about it. There's also no lives and no punishment for taking as many attempts as you need on each level. 

Flaws? Most of the bosses are basically just extra levels. In a game where the levels are spectacular.

Super Meat Boy is a classic for everyone from the 2000s. It's one of the first popular PC platformers that really paved the way for the great platformers we see today. It's simple, but its focus on keeping the pace and flow really makes every try worth it. It's a punishing game in a good sense, you won't be able to complete hard levels on the first tries. It will take you multiple ones to figure out the way the level is supposed to be played and the timings for various interactions. Although your playable character does not unlock new mechanics, the areas get progressively harder and introduce new interactions every time. 

The art gives it personality and even a nostalgic feeling as of today. The story and cutscenes are really in tune with what was normal at the time. You are always in action; there's no dull moment when you are racing against the clock for a better time in very tense levels where one mistake and you have to restart your great run until there. In this sense, it would really benefit from a "Restart level" shortcut in the controls because it gets frustrating to have to die every time you want to restart a level that is not going well timewise.

[h1][u][b]SUPER MEAT BOY: AN INDIE MASTERPIECE[/b][/u][/h1]
(All this review is just my opinion, if you have a different opinion I'd love to read it)

[h3][b][u]Story:[/u][/b] 5/10[/h3] 
Not much of a good story, just save your gf, but the game focus on the gameplay, so it's not a big deal.

[h3][b][u]Characters:[/u][/b] 8/10[/h3] 
Although none of the characters say anything, they're very charming. It's amazing 'cause I've played other games that focus more on their characters and their development, but in the end I don't care about them, while in Super Meat Boy I liked most of the characters. 
 
[h3][b][u]Game art:[/u][/b] 7/10[/h3]
For me, the game art is not that good. However, since it's an indie game and was released in 2010, it deserves a solid 7.

[h3][b][u]Gameplay:[/u][/b] 10/10[/h3]
Simple but excellent. 

[h3][b][u]Level design:[/u][/b] 10/10[/h3]
The level design is great, one of the best I've ever seen in a platform game, although the levels are difficult, if you master the movement you can beat them in less than 1 minute (and it's so satisfying to do so). Also the difficult progression between worlds is smooth.

[h3][b][u]Soundtrack:[/u][/b] 10/10[/h3]
Super Meat Boy's songs are such a banger, each song gets better and better as you progress through the worlds, and they fit perfectly with the speedy feel of the levels. I never get tired of them.

[h3][b][u]Replayability (Not counting achievements):[/u][/b] 8/10[/h3]
Since the very beginning of the game, it offers 4 types of replayability:
[list]
    [*][b]Bandages:[/b] There are bandages in certain levels, you can go and collect them as you play, but it's quite likely that you won't even get half of them before you beat the main story because you don't have enough experience or you don't have a specific character. As you collect the bandages, you unlock characters (from other franchises, which is fockin' awesome), each with different abilities. There are 20 bandages per world, for a total of 100.

    [*][b]A+ grades:[/b] Each level has a timer to beat, if you beat it you'll get the A+ grade and unlock the Dark World version of the level, if you beat all the Dark Worlds you'll get the real ending.

    [*][b]Warpzones:[/b] In every world (except The End and The Cotton Ally) there are 4 warpzones, 3 in the light world and 1 in the dark world. A warpzone is a hidden portal in a level, and when you enter one you'll be teleported to an 8-bit zone, with only 3 levels, but also with only 3 lives per level, if you lose all your lives before passing the 3 levels you'll get kicked out of the portal and have to restart (you can enter it from the map though, since you've already unlocked it). In each warzone there are 2 bandages, except for the character warzone where you play as a special character, and when you beat this warzone you unlock it.

    [*][b]Glitch levels:[/b] These are like warpzones, but there's only one per world, and they only appear after beating the boss of the world. When you replay a level there's a little chance for bandage girl to glitch, when you touch her you'll get teleported to a single 8-bit level, with only 3 lives too. I think beating these levels doesn't contribute the 100% of a world, so you can try to find n' pass a glitch level or not.
[/list]

This game gets a [b]6/10[/b] from me. I really wish Steam had a [i]neutral review[/i] option.
And to be clear: I’m not reviewing the casual playthrough, but a [b]100% achievement[/b] completion, which is basically the whole game.

Super Meat Boy is probably the most popular hardcore platformer out there, and it has been haunting trophy hunters like me ever since its launch. I always knew about the achievements that require clearing all Light and Dark Worlds [i]without dying[/i], which is exactly why I kept postponing this platinum for so long.

Years passed, though, and I got much better at platformers, mostly thanks to playing a ton of [b]IWBTG fangames[/b]. Eventually YouTube started throwing Super Meat Boy videos at me, and I realized: okay, it’s time. [b]Time to go for this platinum.[/b]

Was it hard? [i]Yes.[/i]
Was it fun? [i]Absolutely not.[/i]

I wholeheartedly hate the [b]inertia[/b] and [b]floor sliding[/b] mechanics. Never before have I felt this inconsistent on some of the easiest levels in the game while attempting no death runs. It genuinely feels like someone is holding your movement buttons longer than you actually do.

So, what did I actually [b]like[/b] in this game, and what completely [b]sickened[/b] me?

[h3]Warp Zones[/h3]

Some of them are extremely [spoiler]well hidden[/spoiler]. They always contain either three difficult levels with [i]bandages[/i] to collect, or they introduce a new [i]playable character.[/i]

As for characters, realistically you will mostly play as [b]The Kid[/b], occasionally using [i]VVVVVV[/i] or [i]Naija[/i] to cheese half of certain levels. Bandages, on the other hand, were genuinely fun to collect. Some required you to backtrack all the way to the start of the level and then reach the finish again without dying. Others forced very risky jumps or just staying in the center of projectiles rain.

Overall, this was enjoyable, except for the fact that Warp Zones always give you [i]three lives[/i]. Which does not matter at all, since you can just restart the zone from the map. I honestly wish Warp Zones had no lives whatsoever.

[h3]Dark Worlds[/h3]

Most of the time, they are just Light World layouts, but with way more obstacles and much tighter jumps. Your first attempts will be painful, but unsurprisingly, the more you practice, the easier they become.

[h3]No Death Runs[/h3]

This is where you really should start worrying about your mental health, because if you don’t stop at the right time, this game will destroy you.

For no death runs, you have to clear [b]all 20 levels[/b] of a world [u]without dying[/u] and [i]without leaving the game[/i]. As far as I know, save scumming doesn't work here. However, if you feel like you are about to die, you can [i]pause[/i] instantly, [i]exit[/i] to the map, and [i]restart[/i] the level. Technically, you did not die, you just re-entered the level.

You can also complete the levels in [b]any order you want[/b], which helps a lot. You can get rid of the hardest levels first and then clean up the easier ones.

[h2]HOWEVER[/h2]

This tactic doesn't work for Cotton Alley Dark World.

I do not know what went wrong with this world, but it feels genuinely [b]unfair[/b]. It is packed with extremely risky levels that are wildly inconsistent in terms of no death success. Sometimes I could clear levels 13-20 flawlessly, only then die on level 5 [i](Waiting Room)[/i] which is ironically one of the slowest levels in the entire world.

After getting the platinum, I honestly never want to touch this game ever again.
And I won’t even wish such poor destiny to my worst enemies.

Super Meat Boy is a platformer game developed by Team Meat and released on PC in 2010. The game has garnered critical acclaim for its challenging gameplay, tight controls, and quirky humor.

The game's premise is simple: players take on the role of Meat Boy, a sentient block of meat who must rescue his girlfriend, Bandage Girl, from the clutches of the evil Dr. Fetus. The game's levels are designed to be incredibly difficult, with players facing a variety of obstacles and hazards as they make their way through each stage.

One of the standout features of Super Meat Boy is its controls. The game's mechanics are tight and responsive, making it easy for players to execute precise movements and jumps. This is crucial, as the game's levels require a high level of skill and precision to complete.

The game's art style is also worth mentioning. The game features a retro-inspired aesthetic, with pixelated graphics and a chiptune soundtrack. The game's humorous tone adds an extra layer of charm, with plenty of jokes and pop culture references to keep players entertained.

Overall, Super Meat Boy is a fantastic platformer that's well worth playing. Its challenging gameplay, tight controls, and quirky humor make it a standout game that's sure to delight fans of the genre. If you're looking for a fun and challenging platformer, Super Meat Boy is definitely worth checking out.

[h1]Amazing classic platforming game with very satisfying difficulty and precision controls[/h1]
Game is all about arcade gameplay, no downtime, no story, no dialogue. Just pure gameplay that rewards timing and precision. Trial, error and speedrun.

The level of challenge is excellent and I had a lot of fun with the game and enjoyed every single second of it. The difficulty is greatly tuned, level design is awesome and the music is also good. 
Despite some challenging stages, I never felt actual frustration with the game because it is so greatly designed that everything feels achievable with practice. The controls feel great, responsive, fast and precise. Every stage can be completed in less than a minute, allowing very fast paced progression.

Honestly, I did not feel the game as difficult as everyone says, but that is my opinion. I like games with higher difficulty and value gameplay controls and responsiveness with high regards in videogames.
Videogames should be videogames, with gameplay. This may sound obvious, but at this day and age, we live in an era where videogames are more like interactive movies, with super easy gameplay to reach mainstream audience and extreme hand-holding. Which contrasts a lot with the old era where every game was made for arcades and purposefully made to be challenging and difficult, and Super Meat Boy captures this old arcade difficulty style incredibly well.

The game took me only 4.7 hours to beat by completing all normal levels until the last boss and I see there is still more post-game content in an extra chapter.

For comparison with other difficult platformers, I'd say Super Meat Boy is more difficult than Celeste, but less difficult than Geometry Dash.

For the price on sale being less than can of coke at less than $1, Super Meat Boy is absolutely worth it to have in the collection.

[h3] Super Meat Boy is the hardest and yet most chill game I’ve played. [/h3]

Super Meat Boy is seen as ‘traditionally’ difficult, but it’s by far the [i] least [/i] frustrating game I’ve played. There are no cheap deaths; the game is open about its obstacles and often gives you plenty of time to navigate them, just don’t panic. But that’s the key: you have to relax.

To me, frustration is about not being in control. When we are punished by things which we had no input or say on, we feel helpless and, in turn, our confidence falters. When our confidence drops, we make [i] more [/i] mistakes. We blame ourselves, and our self-esteem drops. What turns into an external problem, becomes an internal one - and we feel bad about ourselves and our inadequacies. 

Super Meat Boy’s gamepad controls are so responsive, Meat Boy so agile, and momentum so quick to adjust that you always feel in control. Even when you make a mistake and miss the perfect opportunity to jump, there’s always a split second where quick thinking and calm nerves can fix the situation. Short stages and instant, unlimited respawns means you never lose more than a few seconds of progress either, and so you’re never really punished for failure nor are your nerves fried from the pressure. 

Once you’ve cracked the exact timings to a jump, or exact moment to slide down a wall, you’ve completed one of 5 to 10 ‘mini’ challenges in each level, and it’s just a matter of stringing them altogether. Easier said than done, but muscle memory picks up the slack where your brain might usually get tired. And if you do feel like it’s getting too easy, Super Meat Boy has a ‘B-side’ (known as the dark world) to every level which offers a challenging new twist on the original concept. This is most interesting in the first stage of the game, where a basic tutorial can suddenly doubles into a playground for advanced techniques.

Placed sneakily within regular levels are special stages which flip the formula, at least visually. These include levels themed around the monochromatic original Gameboy, the NES, or even the Windows blue screen of death. These bonus levels are a breath of fresh air, but can occasionally edge towards the frustrating. Most include limited lives, bringing an unexpected level of punishment for trial and error, and the visual style can make obstacles difficult to discern from the background.

Overall, Super Meat Boy is a fast-n-fantastic platformer brimming with charm and personality. The game’s quality rarely slips, and it’s abundance of content can keep you addicted indefinitely. I wholeheartedly recommend, as well as ‘Indie Game: The Movie’ which covers the highs and lows of its development.
